comments.text:
Some interesting points, but they oversimplify a complex evolution.  Much of China's development and growth (especially land conquest) happened during the Yuan and Qing dynasties.  Those two dynasties were ruled by non-Han people (the Mongolians and the Manchurians).  Because both dynasties were ruled by non-Han ethnic minorities that had to govern a massive Han Chinese majority, they had to balance preserving their own elite identities with incorporating diverse populations to maintain stability.   

It was in the best interest of the Yuan and Qing leaders to keep everybody getting along and working together. I believe that those centuries of being ruled by "outsiders" was a driving force in unifying China.

comments.author: @rh5340
comments.text: Politics is more important than anything else. China has had a modern(ish) national bureaucratic system since the Qin dynasty in 221 BCE, and Europe developed this no earlier than the 17th century. The Chinese identity does not exist for much of the history, actually. It was not until WWII that China became a nation-state. The common folks did not have a sense of national belonging; they did not care much about who ruled them. Dynasties rose and fell, and they lived as peasants in isolated villages for centuries. It is the bureaucratic system that binds everything together under a single empire; they manage the taxation, infrastructure, disaster relief and manpower, and the examination system created a channel for upward mobility, which also reinforced Confucianism across the empire. This is the very foundation for a unified China to survive for over 2000 years.

comments.author: @ZaneMK77
comments.text:
Europe possesses six million square kilometers of plains, whereas China has only 1.15 million. Over 37% of modern China's territory is classified as mountainous, compared to just over 10% for Europe. If we use an elevation of 1,000 meters above sea level as the benchmark, more than 33% of China's core agricultural regions lie above this altitude, while the figure for Europe is only about 6%; yet, you conclude that China's unification was solely due to geography making regional fragmentation difficult—a conclusion that is utter nonsense.
A more significant reason lies in the nature of the writing systems: European scripts are based on pronunciation, so when regions split, neighboring countries would—over time—develop distinct writing systems. In China, while it is common for spoken dialects to vary significantly even between places just a few miles apart, the written form remains uniform. This uniformity not only facilitates administration but also fosters a stronger sense of cultural identity.

comments.text:
There are many inaccuracies and omissions to this narrative :

The Roman Empire did not consist of the lands of Europe as we know them today. They did not control the majority of territories north of the Rhein. They gave that up after the defeat at Teutoberg Forest.

The lands of France, Germany, Poland and then through the Sea of Grass all the way to Moscow are not impeded by mountain ranges and present an expanse as easy to unite as much of the Chinese mainland. 
In fact, this ease of access was the whole problem historically in the fact that Russia was always so open to invasion and had to depend on its vastness to survive.
So there is no geographical reason that much of Europe could not have become one vast nation as China did, less a few archipelagos like Italy, just as Korea never became permanently part of China (the northern half was part of China during the Han Dynasty).
Sichuan is divided from the rest of China by mountains and forests which is why it was always the bolt hole for emperors fleeing war and conquest, but nevertheless, it remained part of the nation through the centuries.

On the other hand, the various kingdoms of Europe remained fiercely independent and eventually developed national identities which they regarded as entirely distinct from the others. 
This remains the case to this day.
On the other hand, after the Han Dynasty, however China fragmented, all the fragments regarded unity as the natural and desirable state : they simply had different ideas as to who was the legitimate ruler. And thus, they all fought to reunify the land. 
Moreover, every conqueror, from the Xianbei to the Mongols to the Manchus would take up the mantle of Chinese civilisation and come to see themselves as the legitimate inheritors of the civilisational state.

The mountains never prevented the Roman Empire from controlling the “Archipelagos” of Spain and Italy and binding them to the empire for centuries. 
Nor did the Mediterranean prevent them from controlling Egypt and North Africa.
So this points to other factors at work.

The Qin Emperor was instrumental in knitting the country together by building a vast network of roads and canals like the Romans did.
But he also standardised axel widths (so that where there were no paved roads, the ruts would act as tracks).
He standardised the written language throughout the empire.
He standardised weights and measures and the currency.

The Eastern Roman Empire continued to speak and write in Greek rather than Latin throughout the history of the Roman Empire, and when Constantinople took over as the capital, Greek became the main language of administration.

The Drachm remained the currency of the Eastern part of the Roman Empire as well as in Egypt (which had been under Greek rule), and the Romans did not impose their currency.

Rome did not standardise axel widths as the Qin empire did.

There were not standard weights and measures in the Roman Empire, which continued to use different standards in all their various regions.

When the Roman Empire broke apart, no succeeding polity ever gained the power to impose their administration throughout the kingdoms of Europe.

China is not nearly as accessible as implied by this program : the Southern part of China is riddled with rivers which meant that cavalry could not simply race unimpeded over the plains : this presented huge obstacles to the subjugation of the south, and they had to develop river fleets and the attendant technology in order to do so.

comments.text: 作为一个中国人，我想说主要原因还是地理因素，其次是中原文明的高度发展，对周边文明具有吸引力，至于文字，在秦始皇统一中国之前，天下的文字就是一样的，因为天下都遵奉一个天子，从夏朝开始到周朝，更像是一个联邦制国家，各地区高度自治，但领袖只是国王，所有的国王都有一个统一的领导，就是天子，秦始皇不过是打破了这种格局罢了，奠定了后期的家天下雏形。

replies.author: @dlkjusdjfhur
replies.text: 关于地理因素，中国的西部地区有着天然的屏障，数千公里的盐碱地，无人区，沙漠，雪山，虽然阻止了欧洲地区军队的侵略，但也阻止了中国军队向西的探索，北边是西伯利亚荒原，东边是大海，最南边又是数不尽的雨林和烟瘴，这使得所有中国的统治者只需要专心在有限的范围内行动，另一方面，这片土地应有尽有，拿到中国的统治权后，你没必要再往更远处探索，最明显的例子就是明朝，用世界最大的海军探索了地球很多角落，最后还是选择回到中国并决定不再出去探索。

comments.author: @annamorning
comments.text:
Geography is definately an important factor, but I don't think that only is enough. As others have mentioned, unified writing system definitely is another. 
I also want to point to the self reinforcing power of the precedence. In Chinese history, any king, emperor during a dividing period is expected to have ambition to reunit - no matter how small or large his control land is. At least the ruler must say so, even if it's just lip services. Otherwise the people serving under that ruler will look down on him and may look into alternative. 😅 

On the other hand, European rulers don't usually carry that burden. That's an extra bonus.
